title: Focker-In-Law isn't terrible. It's just a sitcom
summary: Focker-In-Law is nothing compared to 2000's Meet the Parents. But if comparing to the intentionally broad, necessarily formulaic situation-comedy field the bloated Fockers franchise has found itself…

image.caption: This image released by Universal Pictures and Paramount Pictures shows Ben Stiller, left, and Ariana Grande in a scene from Focker In-Law. (Universal Pictures/Paramount)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

Focker-In-Law is nothing compared to 2000's Meet the Parents. But if comparing to the intentionally broad, necessarily formulaic situation-comedy field the bloated Fockers franchise has found itself in, it's ... fine? Mostly? Watchable, let's say. And that's all these things are going for.
Ben Stiller, Ariana Grande-led instalment of Meet the Parents franchise deliver middling, serviceable comedy
There is a fairly simple way to avoid seeing how far the mighty have fallen. Just avoid finding out where they fell from.

When it comes to the probably-too-cutely-titled Fockers franchise, that seems to be the recipe for success. Because following 2010's Little Fockers, 2004’s Meet the Fockers and finally, the normally titled comedy that started it all, 2000's Meet the Parents, there’s really only one way to avoid disappointment: Only watch the entries earning their buck off the punny name of our titular Gaylord (though he'd much prefer you call him Greg) Focker. Or skip them all and just stick to the seminal indie smash success whose title didn’t lean on him at all.

Clearly, some critics didn't take this advice when heading into Focker-In-Law, the newest iteration of the Ben Stiller-led comedy premise. So far holding the second-lowest Rotten Tomatoes score of the critically panned sequels, the film's dour reception appears to broadly circle the same complaints. Too broad. Too cliche. And — aside from the bubbly Focker-in-law herself, Ariana Grande — too dour. That means you, Ben Stiller.

That, though, is true only if you don't judge it on face value. Because really, what else did you expect? If it was for a return to the heights of Jay Roach's "original" — itself a sort-of remake of the 1992 comedy of the same name — you're out of luck. But if comparing it to the intentionally broad, necessarily formulaic, situation-comedy field that the bloated Fockers franchise has found itself in, it's ... fine? Mostly? Watchable, let's say. And that's all these things are going for.

Because more than 25 years after his famously awkward, increasingly idiotic protagonist turned a meeting with exacting father-in-law Jack (Robert De Niro) into a cavalcade of I Love Lucy-esque disasters of his own moronic making, Greg is left with few to no grounded choices. What else to do but what director/co-writer (and Zoolander co-writer) John Hamburg opted for here: a feud between overbearing Greg and his son (Skyler Gisondo) Henry's impossibly perfect, ex-hostage-negotiator girlfriend, Olivia (Grande)?

If you're waiting for some type of subversion, keep waiting. The central conflict — and its resolution — is about as hard to guess as what, exactly, Samuel L. Jackson is going to find in the cockpit in Snakes on a Plane.

Take it from Greg's long-suffering wife, Pam (Teri Polo), to whom director Hamburg even needs to give an expositional line about how Greg only acts this insane on family trips. (If not, why wouldn't she have divorced him yet?) Greg is now older than Jack was during the events of the first film. Wouldn't it be crazy if it were his turn to play the Jack to his own son's new flame?

Cue the most basic, least innovative evolution to allow this repeated framing to occur, once again. Greg is now the one to suggest strapping Olivia into the lie detector chair, to battle Olivia in a bizarrely high-stakes race by unsuspecting pedestrians (though this time on ludicrously slow bikes instead of sedans).

But there's one new complication thrown into the mix, in that all the while, he's still desperately and pathetically trying to earn the affections of his family — and of Jack, which he attempts with unsettling, pseudo-romantic passion.
This image released by Universal Pictures and Paramount Pictures shows Ben Stiller, left, and Robert De Niro in a scene from Focker In-Law. (Atsushi Nishijima/Universal Pictures)
The solution

For high-concept features doomed by both their initial originality and unexpected success, there are few options to keep them rolling as a series. And, as Fockers' consistent box office success in the face of equally consistent negative reviews shows, there's one method that can keep at least the money rolling in: Become a sitcom.

That is, figure out a way to put your characters in the exact same situation with the near-exact same logline as before. For The Hangover, simply lose a different friend — or have him kidnapped this time. In Home Alone, perform a narrative reset by losing Kevin all over again. But have him lose his parents instead. And always: have every character constantly remark on how ridiculous it is this is all happening again, so the audience doesn't have to.

The sitcom format works for television, as the pilot is expected to showcase a formula to revisit later. But it's different for film, where the original is expected to be its own self-contained story. How do you have your character face the same problem again when previous entries had them surmount whatever central flaw brought the problem about in the first place?

blocks.text: If you're Home Alone, it's simple: Just get a new kid for the (somehow) four sequels beyond Macaulay Culkin. For Focker-In-Law, the solution is even simpler: Have Greg revert to the same psychotically self-conscious behaviour he's exhibited in every film so far, despite the character development with which the previous films ostensibly all ended.

While Jack has long ago accepted him into his coveted "circle of trust," Focker-In-Law continues to set up hypothermia-inducing ice-plunges and pants-ripping dog attacks largely around Greg's obsessive need to continue impressing him.

And the rest of the cast is left as shallow supporting acts to gawk at the unbelievably short-sighted choices made by this grown man, who presumably has a 401(k) and a consistently paid mortgage, yet also just burned his eyebrows off after pouring nearly a full bottle of whisky onto a flaming pan.

There is the parallel plotline: Greg's competition with Olivia's funny — if, once again, one-dimensional — and powerful perfectionism. In fact, the only person who seems to have changed much is Jack. Previously a meat-eating traditionalist, this Jack is now, inexplicably, a vegan on a health kick who immediately takes to Olivia and Henry's relationship, arguing that sexually active couples should be allowed to share a room and even complimenting the gorgeous vegan meal she cooks as Greg's burnt steak smoulders untouched on the plate.

This image released by Universal Pictures and Paramount Pictures shows, from left, Eduardo Franco, Beanie Feldstein, Teri Polo, Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller in a scene from Focker In-Law. (Atsushi Nishijima/Universal Pictures)

This does work against Focker-In-Law's success in a vacuum. Where Greg's neuroses could be excused when he was up against an unbelievable monster, he becomes much harder to empathize with when up against normal humans. A doubly strange double-down: Stiller's protagonist genuinely becomes the least likeable player in his own movie.

Still, the undeniable unoriginality is not enough to make Focker-In-Law unwatchable. Greg's daughter's live-in boyfriend, Eduardo (Eduardo Franco), endears with the hilariously earnest patter he showed off in his criminally short turn in Stranger Things.

Then there is Grande's typical, unflappable comedic timing, which picks up the pace whenever things really start to drag. And there is the no longer novel yet ever-present formula, reheated and presented once more.
Again, it's nothing even close to the serviceable, interesting first entry, in a franchise that should probably now be sorted by pre- and post-Focker. But otherwise, it is … fine?
